narrative_purpose: Makes the carbonate budget concrete: on one reef, some organisms add limestone while others remove it, and the balance decides the reef's fate.
subject: A single continuous reef scene divided by activity rather than by a border. On the left, healthy branching and massive coral-analogue colonies and a spreading crust of pink encrusting coralline algae are visibly laying down bright pale limestone. On the right, a large parrotfish-analogue with a beaked jaw scrapes a bite from the reef surface leaving a fresh white scar, and a cutaway of the same rock shows dark tunnels and cavities bored through it by sponges and worms hollowing it from within.
scene: One reef flat in clear shallow water, builders concentrated left, eroders right, drifting rubble in between.
camera: Wide straight-on plate at reef scale, both processes at equal visual weight.
light: Cyan glow on the living building corals and coralline crust, cooler neutral light on the scraped and bored right side, indigo in the borings.
palette: Ocean teal and cyan on the builder side, muted stone-grey and magenta accents on the eroder side, void indigo cavities.
style: Painterly naturalist comparison plate, organic, not an infographic.
detail_level: Crisp on the fresh limestone, the parrotfish bite scar and the sponge borings; open water above framed by deep negative space.
composition: Left-to-right builder-vs-eroder layout with open low-detail water bands above each side for overlay labels.
consistency_notes: Both sides are the SAME reef, same palette. The parrotfish-analogue is a reef fish, not an Earth species portrait. Coralline algae read as pink encrusting crust.
negative_prompt: no text, no labels, no arrows, no plus/minus symbols, no scale icon, no photographic or 3D-render look, no cartoon style
